title: How do you solve a profitability case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete profitability case guide: the structure, a worked bakery case with real numbers, the mistakes that cost candidates, and practice prompts.
hook: Profitability cases are the most common case of all, so it pays to see one solved properly, with real numbers, from the first question to the final recommendation. This guide pulls together the structure, a fully worked example and the mistakes we see candidates make most often.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet this case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example with real numbers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Phrases to use
  • Practice prompts with model answers

When you will meet this case

Profits are falling, or the client wants them higher.

The structure

Is it revenue, costs or both? Is the whole industry hit, or just us?
  • Revenue (revenue = units × price)
    • Units sold (customers × purchases each)
    • Price per unit
  • Costs
    • Fixed costs (rent · salaried staff · overheads)
    • Variable costs (materials · delivery · commissions)

Split every line by product, customer segment and channel: a shift in mix often hides inside the averages. Compare each line with competitors to tell a company problem from a market problem.

A fully worked example

The prompt: a regional bakery chain's revenue has been flat at £20M for two years, but profit fell from £2M to £1.2M. Why, and what should it do?

Step 1: split the change. Revenue is flat, so the £0.8M fall must be costs. Ask for the cost lines over the two years:

Cost lineTwo years agoNowChange
Ingredients£6.0M£6.2M+£0.2M
Staff£7.0M£7.1M+£0.1M
Rent£2.0M£2.0M0
Delivery app commissions£0.5M£1.0M+£0.5M
Other£2.5M£2.5M0

Step 2: find the driver. Commissions explain £0.5M of the £0.8M. Delivery sales doubled from £2M to £4M, and the apps charge 25%. But total revenue did not grow, so in-store sales must have fallen by £2M. Customers moved from the counter to the app.

Step 3: the so what. Each £1 that moves from in-store to delivery now costs 25p in commission. Delivery is not bringing new customers; it is the same customers paying the bakery less.

Recommendation: "Profit fell mainly because sales moved to delivery apps, which cost 25% commission without adding revenue. I'd raise delivery menu prices by 10 to 15%, push app customers to click-and-collect with a small discount, and review which shops need delivery at all. Next, I'd check whether ingredient costs are rising faster than competitors'."

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Jumping to cost-cutting ideas before checking whether revenue or costs moved.
  2. Treating revenue as one number instead of splitting it by channel, product or region.
  3. Finding the driver (commissions) but not explaining why it matters (no new customers).
  4. Ending with a list of ideas rather than one clear recommendation and its impact.

Phrases to use

Revenue is flat, so the whole profit fall sits in costs. Could I see the cost lines over the period?
Commissions explain over 60% of the fall, so I'd like to understand the delivery channel next.

Practise with these prompts

A national bank's mortgage applications are down 20% this year. Why?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Total applications in the market: rates, house prices, transactions; Is everyone down 20%, or just us?
  • Our offer: Rates and fees vs rivals; Loan-to-value limits, product range
  • Channels: Brokers: are they placing less with us?; Online and branch: traffic, conversion
  • Process: Time to decision, approval rate (brokers avoid slow or strict lenders); Drop-off during the application

Where to start: The market first: if all banks are down 20%, it is not our problem to fix.

The trap: Jumping to marketing ideas before checking whether the whole market fell.

A ski resort's profits fell 40% after two warm winters.

Show a model structure
  • Winter revenue: Visitors × spend, by month; Lift passes, ski school, food, rentals
  • Costs: Fixed costs: lifts, staff, maintenance; Variable and snow-related: snowmaking, energy
  • Snow risk: Days open, altitude, snowmaking coverage; Trend or two bad years? Share of revenue pre-sold as season passes
  • Non-ski income: Summer, events, conferences; Year-round use of lifts, hotels and restaurants

Where to start: Days open: warm winters cut the season, and costs are mostly fixed.

The trap: Treating it as a normal profit decline and missing that weather is the root cause.

A pharma company's new drug is selling 40% below forecast.

Show a model structure
  • Doctors: Awareness and trust in the data; Who prescribes: specialists vs family doctors
  • Patients: How many are diagnosed and eligible; was the forecast realistic?; Price, side effects, stopping early
  • Payers: Approval for reimbursement; Restrictions: only after other drugs fail
  • Competition: Rival drugs and generics; Their pricing and contracts

Where to start: Payers: if insurers restrict it, doctors and patients can do little.

The trap: Assuming it is a marketing problem when access and reimbursement usually decide.
